rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The King's Guard
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a candlelit royal bedchamber at night with a sick king asleep under embroidered covers, a boy in miner's clothes standing guard with folded arms and a short sword, a huge grey winged creature lying across the door like a rug with one amber eye open, a small golden-haired princess tiptoeing in with a cup, warm candle glow against deep blue shadow, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The city woke up changed. The wicked ministers were locked away where they could hurt nobody, and the King lay quietly in his great bed with his little daughter Irene keeping watch. With the poison stopped, he grew a little stronger every single day.

Curdie was made a guard of the King's chamber, and Lina slept across his door like a great grey rug. But his strange gift kept working all the same. When grand folk came smiling to ask after the King, Curdie shook their hands — and under his fingers he felt brutes, and monkeys, and cold snakes. The city was not healed. It had only begun to be found out.
A miner's boy keeps watch by the King's bed, and Lina guards the door.
Ask your child: Curdie's hands feel what people are becoming inside. Why might the old princess give him that gift instead of a sword? Talk about it together.

One morning a silver-white pigeon tapped at the chamber window and dropped a fresh rose leaf on the sill. Curdie knew what that meant: the old princess in her mountain tower was watching. And when he held the leaf, words seemed to breathe out of it: The poison will come in a cup. Watch the wine.

So Curdie watched, night after night, with Lina's eyes glowing in the dark beside him. Princess Irene came softly in to sit with her father, and to bring the guard hot soup on a tray. Between them — boy, princess, and creature — the sleeping King had the finest watch in all the kingdom.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Cup of Wine
chapters.artPrompt: a grand dining anteroom at night where a soft-spoken butler in fine livery pours from a silver jug and only clear water splashes into a golden goblet, his face turning pale grey, a miner boy standing firm in the doorway with a huge grey creature bristling behind him, a sick king stirring in the shadows, tense amber candlelight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The King's wine came up from the cellar every evening, carried by the butler — a grand, soft-spoken man whose hand felt, to Curdie, exactly like a toad's cold belly. One night the butler came early and smiling, with the cup on a silver tray and three grand friends trailing behind him.

Curdie knew the smell of that wine was wrong. He stood in the doorway, as big as he could make himself. 'The King drinks nothing tonight that has not passed my hands first,' he said. The butler's smile went stiff as a mask, and Lina's tail swept the floor once, slowly.
The drugged wine turns to clear water, right before their eyes.
Ask your child: a toad hand and a grand smile can belong to the same person. How can you be polite AND careful, the way Curdie is? Talk about it.

Then the strange thing happened. The butler poured the wine before the King, to shame the boy — and nothing came out of the jug but clear water. He poured again. Water, and only water. The butler's face turned the colour of candle tallow, and his grand friends began backing away along the wall.

'Someone has been at the wine,' said Curdie quietly. The King, waking, saw the whole business in a minute, and the butler was taken, and more of the plotters with him. No one had seen the old princess's hand — but Curdie, touching the empty jug, smiled. Some cares are carried for us from very far away.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Beasts in Fine Clothes
chapters.artPrompt: a grey stone city square before a fortified palace gate where a shoving crowd of townsfolk and clerks in dark coats shout and wave, an odd gentle ring of shaggy winged creatures standing perfectly still around a little fallen child, a huge grey creature standing over it like a mother hen, a boy watching from the steps, cold morning light breaking warm, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The friends of the wicked ministers did not give up. They whispered through the schools and the markets that the King was bewitched, and that a mountain boy and his monsters had stolen the palace. 'Drive out the beasts!' they shouted. 'Drive out the liar!' The shouting grew until it filled the streets.

One grey morning a mob came roaring to the palace gates, and the guards looked at one another and shuffled their feet. Then the Uglies came out — odd, shaggy, gentle — and stood in a quiet ring, with Lina in front, and did nothing at all but stand.
The mob melts away before creatures who will not fight, only stand.
Ask your child: the crowd shouts 'monsters!' — but who behaves like a monster in this chapter? Talk about judging creatures by what they do, not by what they look like.

A little child tumbled in the crush, and Lina broke her own line to stand over it like a mother hen, until its mother snatched it up safe. The crowd saw everything. Roaring is easy; standing still and kind is much harder. The mob grew ashamed, then smaller, then gone — and some honest citizens stayed behind and said so out loud.

'You see,' said Curdie to Lina that evening, scratching her great ears, 'half the battle is only being brave enough to be gentle.' Her tail thumped the floor twice, which with Lina meant yes — and also, do not stop scratching.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The King Sits in Judgment
chapters.artPrompt: a high vaulted royal hall with banners where a pale king sits straight on his throne in judgement, courtiers in fine coats passing one by one before him, a miner boy in rough clothes standing close behind the throne with hands ready, a bent grey-haired miner holding a basket of apples below, shafts of window light on stone, storybook illustration

blocks.text: At last the King was strong enough to rise. He had himself carried to the great hall and set up in judgment, pale but perfectly straight. One by one the servants and lords and merchants came before him, and one by one Curdie stood behind the great chair with his hands ready.

There was no arguing with those hands. A lord who felt like a weasel wept and confessed. A clerk who felt like a magpie gave back the keys he had stolen. An honest baker's hand felt like warm bread, and was trusted with the city's stores before everyone.
The King sits in judgment, and a miner's boy stands behind the chair.
Ask your child: Peter leaves the quiet mountain to stand beside his son in the noisy city. What does he give up, and what does he get? Talk about family sticking together.

And down from the mountains came Peter the miner, grey and bent and proud, to stand beside his son. He had brought apples, and a new scarf knitted by Curdie's mother, and no idea at all of how famous his boy had become. 'The mine never made you vain,' he said, looking about the great hall. 'I see the mountain kept you humble.'

The false servants went away in wagons, and honest folk took their places. The King slept that night without any medicine, and the city walked softer in the morning — like a house where somebody honest is awake.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Goodbye to the Uglies
chapters.artPrompt: a green palace garden at golden evening where a young princess ties bright ribbons round the necks of a line of odd gentle creatures — shaggy, winged, awkward — as they turn toward distant pine mountains, a huge grey creature staying close to a miner boy by the wall, long warm shadows, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Peace sat on the palace at last, like sunshine on a warm wall. The King walked in the garden with Irene, and told her stories, and ate a whole dinner and asked for more. He gave Curdie a place of the greatest honour, and shook Lina's great paw in front of everybody.

But the mountain creatures grew restless. They pined for their caves, and their pine trees, and their dark and quiet. One by one they slipped away over the hills, home — and the palace felt their going like a fire going out on a cold night.
The strange faithful creatures slip away home over the hills.
Ask your child: the Uglies helped best by going home, and Lina helped best by staying. Talk about what makes a helper a friend — being there, or going when the work is done?

Lina stayed. She would not go, though her brothers and sisters called her from the crags all night. She had chosen Curdie, once and for all, and a choice like Lina's does not blow away. She still slept across his door, one eye open, dreaming her wolf-dreams.

Princess Irene gave each departing creature a bright ribbon for its neck, and watched them out of sight. 'Come back someday,' she called — and it seemed to Curdie that the mountain itself answered her, in a far-off rumble like a purr.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Princess and the Miner's Boy
chapters.artPrompt: a high round tower room filled with rose vines and rose-colored fire, a graceful old lady with silver hair kissing the hands of a tall young man in fine clothes, a young princess with golden hair beside him holding a white pigeon, threads of light swirling, radiant and tender scene, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Years went by, the way good years do — quicker than bad ones. Irene grew tall, with her mother's grace and her own brave heart. Curdie grew broad and brown and quiet, and the King said openly that the mountain had sent him a son.

So when the time came, there was no grander wedding in any storybook. The city was hung with ribbons, the Uglies came down the mountainside in their oddest best, and Lina walked before the bride with her wings spread out like a canopy.
Before the wedding, the old grandmother blesses them with rose-colored fire.
Ask your child: the gift that hurt a little at first turned into a gift of love. Talk about something hard that taught you to understand people better.

First, though, they climbed the tower stair, alone. The old princess sat among her roses, younger than spring, and she kissed Curdie's hands once more — gently this time, like cooling embers. 'You felt the beasts,' she said. 'Now go and love the people.' The rose-fire burned sweetly, and two white pigeons circled the tower and would not leave.
Then the bells rang out, and Irene and Curdie were married, and the poor had bread at every gate that day. It was a wedding fit for a princess — which is to say, it was fit for a true friend.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · Home to the Mountain
chapters.artPrompt: a small stone cottage with roses at the door on a green mountain slope at sunset, an old silver-haired king and queen in plain clothes walking up the path hand in hand, an old grey winged creature dozing by the door, white pigeons wheeling above pines, a faint rose glow in a distant tower under first stars, storybook illustration

blocks.text: They reigned long and kindly, Curdie and Irene, and the kingdom had peace such as it had not known for a hundred years. But cities change slowly, and even a good city forgets. The grand folk went back to counting gold, and the schools went back to cleverness, and the old wonder faded like morning mist.

So, when they were old and silver-haired, the King and Queen did a strange thing. They crowned no one and made no speech. They put on plain clothes, whistled to Lina — grey now about the muzzle — and walked quietly out of the city and up into the mountains, home.
The old king and queen walk home to a little cottage in the mountains.
Ask your child: the story ends in a cottage, not on a throne. Why do you think Curdie and Irene chose the mountain? What would make a life feel rich to you?

There they lived in a cottage near the old mine, with roses at the door and pigeons from the tower coming and going all day long. The mountain people never learned that they had ever been crowned at all. They knew only that the old couple were kind, and wise, and wonderfully good at telling stories.

And on summer evenings a rose-fire could be seen, some said, glowing in the old tower under the stars. But only the true hearts ever saw it. That, said the story, was always the way of it — and always will be.
